newsitem.title: UK: Another study defends calcium-channel blockers.
newsitem.headline: Another study defends calcium-channel blockers.

text.p: More researchers came to the defence of calcium-channel blockers on Friday, saying the drugs commonly used to treat high blood pressure and heart disease did not seem to cause cancer.
A report last August linking calcium-channel blockers with cancer caused a furore and intense study of the popularly-used drugs ensued.
Dr Hershel Jick and colleagues at Boston University's Medical Centre reported in the Lancet medical journal on Friday that they had found no link between use of the drugs and cancer.

"The small positive association between calcium-channel blockers and risk of cancer is unlikely to be causal since there is no increase in risk with increasing duration of calcium-channel blocker use," they wrote.

They studied 446 patients suffering from hypertension and cancer and 1,750 patients suffering only from high blood pressure, all of whom were taking calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers or angiotensin-converting-enzyme (ACE) inhibitors.
They found a slightly raised risk of cancer among users of the drugs but it did not get worse if they took them for longer.
But they said their study only covered a seven-year period so they did not know if the effect changed over longer periods.
The researchers, funded by Bayer AG which makes the drugs, said there could be some other reason for the slight cancer link.

Last August Marco Pahor of the University of Tennessee in Memphis said the health records of more than 5,000 men and women over the age of 70 showed that those who used calcium-channel blockers were 70 percent more likely to develop cancer.
But Pahor said this did not mean heart disease patients should stop taking the drugs.

A study released at last November's American Heart Association meeting in New Orleans used data from more than 4,000 patients followed for up to 12 years and showed no evidence of increased risk for mortality or cancer.
Calcium-channel blockers help lower blood pressure and ease the heart's workload by preventing calcium accumulating in the muscle cells of the heart and blood vessels.
Sellers of calcium-channel blockers include Pfizer Inc, Bayer AG, Hoechst Marion Roussel Inc., a unit of Hoechst AG, and Astra Merck Inc., a joint venture of Merck & Co Inc and Sweden's Astra AB.
